summary.text: For odd primes, the recurrence \(a(n+1)=(2^n-1)a(n)+2^{\binom{n+1}{2}}\), together with Fermat’s theorem, has coefficients unchanged after a shift of \(2(p-1)\); the shifted base case follows because every summand but the last contains \(2^{2(p-1)}-1\equiv0\pmod p\), while the last is \(1\), so induction applies. For \(p=2\), the same recurrence shows directly that every \(a(n)\) with \(n\ge1\) is odd.

full_proof.text:
Let
\[
a(n)=\sum_{k=0}^{n-1}2^{\binom{k+1}{2}}
       \prod_{j=k+1}^{n-1}(2^j-1),\qquad n\geq 1.
\]
(As usual, an empty product is equal to 1.) We prove that for every prime \(p\) and every \(n\geq 1\),
\[
a\bigl(n+2(p-1)\bigr)\equiv a(n)\pmod p.
\]

First we establish the recurrence that will be used throughout. In the defining sum for \(a(n+1)\), consider first an index \(k<n\). Its product is
\[
\prod_{j=k+1}^{n}(2^j-1)
=(2^n-1)\prod_{j=k+1}^{n-1}(2^j-1).
\]
Thus the sum of all terms with \(k<n\) is \((2^n-1)a(n)\). The one remaining term, corresponding to \(k=n\), has an empty product and is therefore \(2^{\binom{n+1}{2}}\). Hence
\[
\boxed{\ a(n+1)=(2^n-1)a(n)+2^{\binom{n+1}{2}}.\ }
\tag{1}
\]
Also, directly from the definition,
\[
a(1)=2^{\binom12}=1.
\tag{2}
\]

We now split according as \(p=2\) or \(p\) is odd.

### The prime \(p=2\)

We claim that
\[
a(n)\equiv 1\pmod 2\qquad(n\geq 1).
\tag{3}
\]
This is true for \(n=1\) by (2). Suppose it is true for some \(m\geq 1\). Since \(m\geq1\), the number \(2^m-1\) is odd. Moreover,
\[
\binom{m+1}{2}=\frac{m(m+1)}2>0,
\]
so \(2^{\binom{m+1}{2}}\) is even. Reducing (1) modulo 2 therefore gives
\[
a(m+1)\equiv 1\cdot a(m)+0\equiv1\pmod2.
\]
This proves (3) by induction. For \(p=2\), the proposed shift is \(2(p-1)=2\), and both \(a(n+2)\) and \(a(n)\) are congruent to 1 modulo 2. Thus the required result holds in this case.

### Odd primes

Assume from now on that \(p\) is an odd prime, and put
\[
T=2(p-1).
\]
Because \(p\nmid 2\), Fermat's theorem gives
\[
2^{p-1}\equiv1\pmod p.
\tag{4}
\]
Consequently,
\[
2^T=2^{2(p-1)}\equiv1\pmod p.
\tag{5}
\]
It follows immediately that for every \(n\geq0\),
\[
2^{n+T}=2^n2^T\equiv2^n\pmod p.
\tag{6}
\]

We also need periodicity of the inhomogeneous power appearing in (1). The elementary triangular-number identity
\[
\binom{n+2q+1}{2}
= inom{n+1}{2}+q(2n+2q+1)
\tag{7}
\]
holds for all nonnegative integers \(n,q\). Indeed, multiplying both sides by 2 reduces it to the expansion
\[
(n+2q)(n+2q+1)=n(n+1)+2q(2n+2q+1).
\]
Taking \(q=p-1\) in (7), and using (4), we obtain
\[
\begin{aligned}
2^{\binom{n+T+1}{2}}
&=2^{\binom{n+1}{2}+(p-1)(2n+2(p-1)+1)}\\
&=2^{\binom{n+1}{2}}
  \left(2^{p-1}\right)^{2n+2(p-1)+1}\\
&\equiv2^{\binom{n+1}{2}}\pmod p.
\end{aligned}
\tag{8}
\]
Thus both the multiplicative coefficient \(2^n-1\) and the additive term \(2^{\binom{n+1}{2}}\) in recurrence (1) are unchanged modulo \(p\) when \(n\) is increased by \(T\).

To start an induction using this periodic recurrence, we prove directly that
\[
a(1+T)\equiv a(1)\pmod p.
\tag{9}
\]
The defining sum at \(1+T\) is
\[
a(1+T)=\sum_{k=0}^{T}2^{\binom{k+1}{2}}
                 \prod_{j=k+1}^{T}(2^j-1).
\tag{10}
\]
If \(k<T\), then the product in the corresponding summand includes the index \(j=T\), and hence includes the factor
\[
2^T-1\equiv0\pmod p
\]
by (5). Every summand in (10) with \(k<T\) is therefore zero modulo \(p\).

Only the final summand \(k=T\) remains. Its product is empty, so that summand is
\[
2^{\binom{T+1}{2}}.
\]
Writing \(q=p-1\), so that \(T=2q\), we have the second elementary triangular-number identity
\[
\binom{2q+1}{2}=q(2q+1).
\tag{11}
\]
Therefore
\[
2^{\binom{T+1}{2}}
=2^{(p-1)(2(p-1)+1)}
=\left(2^{p-1}\right)^{2(p-1)+1}
\equiv1\pmod p
\]
by (4). It follows from (10) that \(a(1+T)\equiv1\pmod p\), and this equals \(a(1)\) by (2). This proves (9).

We now propagate (9) to every positive index. We prove by induction on \(m\geq1\) that
\[
a(m+T)\equiv a(m)\pmod p.
\tag{12}
\]
The case \(m=1\) is (9). Suppose (12) holds for a given \(m\geq1\). Apply recurrence (1) first at the index \(m+T\):
\[
a(m+T+1)
=(2^{m+T}-1)a(m+T)+2^{\binom{m+T+1}{2}}.
\]
Reducing modulo \(p\), using (6), the induction hypothesis, and (8), gives
\[
\begin{aligned}
a(m+T+1)
&\equiv(2^m-1)a(m)+2^{\binom{m+1}{2}}\\
&=a(m+1)\pmod p,
\end{aligned}
\]
where the final equality is recurrence (1) at index \(m\). This is exactly (12) for \(m+1\), so induction proves (12) for all \(m\geq1\).

Finally, since \(T=2(p-1)\), (12) says precisely that for every odd prime \(p\) and every \(n\geq1\),
\[
a\bigl(n+2(p-1)\bigr)\equiv a(n)\pmod p.
\]
Together with the separate argument for \(p=2\), this proves the assertion for every prime \(p\).
